Subject: Scheduling approach for a multi‑mode, resource‑constrained project

Overview
We are planning a project composed of multiple interdependent activities that must share limited, renewable resources. Each activity can be executed in more than one way, trading speed for cost and resource intensity. The challenge is to choose an execution mode for every activity and arrange their start times so that all dependency and timing requirements are respected, shared resources are managed safely, and total spending stays within the fixed project budget—all while minimizing the overall completion time.

Execution modes and trade‑offs
Each activity has several execution options (modes). Faster modes shorten duration but typically require more resources at once and cost more; slower modes use fewer resources and cost less but prolong the schedule. Only one mode can be selected per activity. This choice affects both how long the activity runs and how it interacts with others competing for the same resources.

Dependencies and timing requirements
Activities are linked by precedence relationships: some must finish before others can begin. Certain links also carry minimum delays (a successor must wait at least a specified time after its predecessor completes) and, in some cases, maximum delays (a successor must start within a specified time window after its predecessor finishes). In addition, some activities cannot start before their earliest allowed start dates, and some must be completed by firm deadlines.

Renewable resources and the conservative safety rule
Resources are renewable: once an activity finishes, the resources it used are released and become available for subsequent work. To safeguard against overloads without continuously monitoring capacity over time, we will apply a conservative safety rule between activities that are not linked by precedence:

- If there exists even one pair of execution modes (one for each activity) and at least one shared resource for which their combined usage would exceed that resource’s capacity, then those two activities cannot run at the same time. They must be sequenced—one must finish before the other starts.
- Where this condition does not hold, the activities may overlap if their other constraints allow.

This pairwise sequencing policy is the only resource constraint we enforce; there is no separate, continuous “at all times” capacity check beyond these conservative overlap decisions. The plan must therefore decide the order for each conflicting independent pair and select modes that balance speed, cost, and resource exposure.

Budget constraint
There is a fixed, non‑renewable project budget. The sum of the costs of the selected modes across all activities must not exceed this cap. Faster modes typically help compress the timeline but consume more budget, so mode selections must be balanced against the budget limit.

Non‑preemptive activities
Once an activity starts, it must run to completion without interruption or mode switching. This simplifies handoffs and resource planning but increases the importance of getting mode and sequencing decisions right up front.

Planning challenge and expected outcomes
Putting these elements together, the schedule must:

- Respect all precedence relationships, including both minimum and, where applicable, maximum delays.
- Honor earliest start dates and meet all hard deadlines.
- Apply the conservative resource safety rule to determine a safe sequence among independent activities that could, in any mode combination, exceed resource capacities.
- Choose exactly one mode per activity such that total mode costs stay within the project budget.
- Minimize the total project duration (makespan) subject to all of the above.

In practice, we will explore mode selections that accelerate critical chains while keeping within budget, and set safe sequencing for independent activities flagged by the safety rule. The result will be a feasible, budget‑compliant plan with a clear, defensible end date and a defined order of work that avoids resource contention.
